summary: Recon for podracer-style Agents Remember dashboard: prototype, branches, issues, data surfaces, inspiration frames, tech research

prototype.architecture: Zero-dependency, single-file HTML apps under dashboard/mockup/ on the branch (working-tree paths would be C:/ew/agents-remember/dashboard/mockup/*; read via git show only). Each file: a CSS design-token contract at :root (full token sheet — colors, type scale, spacing, radii, motion curves) plus a semantic class system, then one vanilla-JS IIFE containing (a) a tiny view router (nav buttons toggle .view.active sections, localStorage persistence, 1-6 keyboard shortcuts), (b) render functions that derive every panel from in-memory JS models, and (c) a Canvas-2D requestAnimationFrame loop for the orbital topology/constellation. Data flow: there is none — no fetch, no WebSocket, no API. mc1 hardcodes data in HTML; mc2 centralizes it in a single-source-of-truth `WS` workspace model (workspace → repos → worktrees{providers[], tasks{steps[], attn}}) plus a `MEM` memory-mirror model, with all six views (tree, counters, attention queue, detail panel, lifecycles table, provider panels, memory tree, topology canvas) derived from those two objects. 'Live' feel is simulated: setInterval random-pool event feed, count-up metric animations, UTC mission clock, fake uptime counter, comets animating along real parent→child graph edges. Theming proven by the variants: the Mistral reskin is ~83 changed lines (tokens only), Operator ~275 (tokens + a tabbed Attention/By-repo/By-lifecycle list refactor + full-height topology layout). prefers-reduced-motion, focus-visible rings, and responsive degrade breakpoints are handled. Provenance: generated by the 'Open Design' web-prototype plugin (nexu-io/open-design, open-design.ai schema), vendored at dashboard/mockup/.od-skills/web-prototype-6b239b831b/ (SKILL.md, assets/template.html seed, references/layouts.md, open-design.json); each HTML has a sibling .html.artifact.json (designSystemId 'spacex') and the PNGs are review screenshots — one (mq0zupso) carries red hand-drawn annotation marks, i.e. a design-iteration loop, not an app codebase.
prototype.branchAge: Single commit: bb0579f 2026-06-05 'mockups' (the only commit not on main). Forked from merge-base 83b147e (2026-06-04, PR #34 / MCP 2.3.3 release). main has since advanced 32 commits to ab7e21b (2026-06-10, PR #59, MCP 2.7.0) — so the branch is ~5 days / 32 commits / four MCP minor releases behind. It is purely additive (25 new files, +6129 lines, all under dashboard/, zero modifications to existing files), so it would still merge cleanly, but its content references stale state (rail footer says 'MCP v2.3.1', and a fictional second repo 'coordination-workbench').
prototype.stack: No framework, no build tool, no package.json — four standalone self-contained HTML files (vanilla ES5-style JS in an IIFE + inline CSS), ~58-95KB each. Charts/visuals are entirely hand-rolled: Canvas 2D for the animated orbital constellation/topology map; DOM+CSS for sparklines, segmented coverage bars, load histograms, pipeline steppers (no chart library). Styling is a CSS-custom-property design-token system with three complete skins: 'SpaceX' (pure black, D-DIN, white accent), 'Mistral' (cream #fffaeb, orange #fa520f, Arial), and 'Operator' (oklch graphite slate + electric cyan-teal, Inter/JetBrains Mono — explicitly 'Linear/Datadog' styled). Scaffolding came from the Open Design (open-design.ai / nexu-io) 'web-prototype' agent skill vendored on the branch.

prototype.verdict: Rebuild — but treat mc2-operator as the approved design spec and harvest it aggressively. These files are design artifacts by construction (Open Design single-file prototype skill, .artifact.json sidecars, hand-annotated review screenshots), with no data layer, no components, and four divergent forks; 'evolving' a 95KB innerHTML-concatenation HTML file into a live, maintainable cockpit would cost more than starting clean and would inherit XSS-prone rendering. The branch's real value is that it already solved the two hardest problems for a high-craft animated cockpit: (1) the information architecture — Operations + Attention Queue as the home screen, Lifecycles/Providers/Memory Health/Retrieval as drill-downs, the orbital Topology map as the hero — and (2) the visual language — the proven oklch token system and a polished, portable canvas topology renderer. Concrete path: new app under dashboard/ with Vite + a typed framework, port WS/MEM model shapes into a real status API on the Python MCP server (HTTP/SSE or WS bridge), lift the Operator token sheet and the buildConstel/layout/frame canvas code into components, and keep the mockups in-repo as the reference (minus the 2.2MB PNGs). Decide mc1-vs-mc2 explicitly: mc2's model-driven 6-view IA supersedes mc1; mc1 contributes only the memory-constellation variant of the canvas and the jump-card overview pattern. The branch itself is purely additive and 32 commits behind — fine to leave parked; nothing on it needs rebasing, only harvesting.

branches.name: ar/observer-runtime-and-tui
branches.purpose: Adds the complete observability stack for Agents Remember: an append-only JSONL event contract, a Python runtime engine that reduces events into a resolved workspace state tree, and a Textual terminal dashboard (TUI) that renders that state. Explicitly designed so 'every frontend does not reimplement lifecycle assembly' — i.e. it defines the data feed any future UI (including a browser dashboard) consumes.
branches.contents: 2 commits ahead of main: 3810326 'Add observer runtime and TUI' and 8d2fbe3 'Handle locked observer event log reads'. Diff vs merge-base: 26 files, +5,677/-10. Key files: docs/observer-event-contract.md (175 lines), docs/observer-runtime-engine.md (153), docs/observer-tech-stack.md (125); events/schema.py (Pydantic envelope 'ar-observer-event/v1' with eventId, dotted-lowercase type, severity, trust=declared|observed|inferred|approved, correlation {workspaceId, sessionId, runId, lifecycleId, operationId, taskId, repoName, worktreeId}, producer, payload), events/emitter.py (append-one-JSON-line-with-lock writer), events/event_cli.py, events/read_session.py, events/adapters/{read_pair,workflow}.py; runtime/engine.py (756 lines, ObserverRuntimeEngine: discovers <coordination_root>/observer/, tails events.jsonl, dedupes by eventId, groups by correlation.lifecycleId, classifies events into lifecycle kinds, merges facts, marks stale sessions, computes metrics and precomputed action availability with disabledReason/nextSafeAction, atomically writes latest-state.json + latest-metrics.json); runtime/schemas.py, runtime/status.py ('observer status' diagnostics without opening the TUI), runtime/clients.py (TUI client leases with TTL). Event families: runtime.session.*, runtime.heartbeat, skill.*, context.resolve.*, drift.scan/file/report.*, onboarding.pair/source/file/maintenance.*, read.session.* (declared read batches), memory.health.*, worktree.status.reported, approval.required/granted/rejected, closeout.*, validation.*, blocker.*, plus append-only corrections (correction.recorded, problem.reopened). State surface 'ar-observer-state/v1': lifecycle arrays agents, sessions, repos, tasks, worktrees, readPairs, readSessions, driftScans, validations, approvals, closeouts, integrations, cleanupRuns, reverseRequests, blockers, activity, plus actions and metrics. TUI: yes — tui/app.py (1,164 lines, Textual ObserverDashboard with tabs Overview/Activity/Reads/Work/Diagnostics, kind/progress/status filter cycling, refresh, seeded fixture mode `python -m tui.app --seeded`, graceful degradation when Textual absent) + tui/styles.tcss; launched via `python -m tui.app --coordination-root <ar-management> --settings-path .../settings.json`. Also: requirements-observer.txt (pydantic, textual), observer settings block added to system/settings.example.json (enabled/workspaceId/privacy/retention maxDays:1 maxMegabytes:250 staleSessionSeconds:1800), event emission instrumented into existing scripts (check_onboarding_drift.py, git_worktree_manager.py, ar_management_resolver.py), and a 1,240-line test file (test_observer_support.py). Note: local branch backup/observer-runtime-and-tui-accidental-closeout is a backup of this same work.
branches.dashboardRelevance: This is THE branch that matters for a browser dashboard — it already defines the live data feed end to end. The runtime engine is the single owner of lifecycle interpretation; docs/observer-runtime-engine.md states latest-state.json 'is the resolved UI model' and frontends must consume it rather than raw events. A browser dashboard would either (a) read/poll <coordination_root>/observer/latest-state.json + latest-metrics.json, (b) tail events.jsonl via the existing tail_events(offset) API behind a thin HTTP/WebSocket server, or (c) reuse ObserverRuntimeEngine.build_state() server-side. The docs also pre-specify the dashboard views (workspace overview, agents/sessions, repos/branches, tasks/worktrees, read pairs/onboarding usage, memory health/drift, validations, approvals/blockers, lifecycle detail, event timeline), trust-provenance rendering rules ('do not pretend declared events are observed'), precomputed action availability (the UI must not infer whether closeout/approval actions are safe), and a reverse-channel request inbox for future UI-initiated actions — all directly reusable as the browser dashboard's product spec. The Textual TUI is effectively dashboard v1 over the same contract; a browser dashboard is frontend v2. Caveat: branch is unmerged and based ~136 commits behind current main, so it needs a rebase before building on it.

relevantIssues.title: worktree_start branches from stale local bases without checking they are current
relevantIssues.relevance: THE open worktree_start bug — the actual issue behind the active branch 'issue-54-stale-bases'. Directly matches the 'worktree_start bugs' sweep keyword and is the remaining open worktree_start fix.
keyPoints: Observed live on 2.5.1: a fresh worktree silently branched from stale bases on BOTH sides — local code main was at 6beccd0 (2.5.0) while origin/main was at 642cca1 (2.5.1), so the worktree was missing the whole 2.5.1 release incl. tool_reports.py; memory main was 2 commits behind because the official memory repo was still on the prior cycle's source branch (fix/tool-hangs-and-budgets)
Root cause 1: worktree_start does not verify the code source branch is current with its remote tracking branch before branching

Root cause 2: nothing in the cycle advances memory main when the cycle ran on a non-main source branch — code main advances via PR merge but memory has no PR flow (worktree_integrate lands onto the source branch; memory_carryover_apply commits onto the checked-out branch), leaving memory main behind indefinitely

Fix candidates: (1) worktree_start preflight fetch + refuse/warn-loudly when the source branch (code or memory branch point) is behind its remote; (2) memory_carryover_apply should fast-forward memory main when the official line is ahead, or closeout/integrate should return the official memory checkout to main ff'd

Comment (2026-06-10): live impact evidence — the stale base also silently defeats the CGC seed mechanic: codegraphcontext seed refuses with 'source and target repository HEAD commits differ' (workspace 592274a vs stale worktree 6beccd0), forcing a cgc refresh-all full reindex at 240.86s instead of a ~1-minute start (GrepAI clone-db 4.8s, Ollama model seed 18.3s), which combined with #53's silence reads as a hung tool
Manual recovery was clean this time (git fetch origin main:main + ff memory main + reset fresh branches), no data loss

uiSequences.label: Circular gauge with red alert wedge, whip-pan to overheating engine schematic
uiSequences.description: Close-up of the cockpit instrument pod. A convex circular CRT gauge shows a dark amber dial: broken outer ring with three Aurebesh glyphs at 12 o'clock, an inner C-shaped tick-mark ring, bright yellow wedge segments at 3 o'clock (level arcs), a center horizontal pill indicator with one lit amber cell, and a glowing red-orange triangular wedge at 6 o'clock acting as an alarm lamp. Left of it, a second rectangular readout shows rows of yellow bar-chart blocks. The camera then whip-pans (frames 216126/216162 are pure horizontal motion blur) onto an oval screen with a single engine drawn as a thin amber wireframe; hot orange-white blotches bloom and spread inside the engine outline across 216180-216243, reading as an animated overheat/damage flicker at roughly 2-3 pulses per second.
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Deep brown-black CRT domes in weathered grey cast-metal bezels; 1-2 px desaturated gold/amber linework; saturated red-orange (#FF4A20) alarm wedge; bright yellow segment fills; Aurebesh-style geometric glyphs; convex-glass specular bloom and halation; whip-pan motion blur implies the gauges sit inches apart on the dash

uiSequences.label: Engine boot-up: dead gauge ignites a sigil, then arcs fill green/blue
uiSequences.description: Two-gauge boot sequence. At 216468 the near gauge is OFF: only a dull brick-red broken ring with notched tabs, two small glowing red dots on the ring, a faint tick ring, and an empty red alert box at lower right - the screen face is black. At 216486-216504 a swirling orange sigil (a calligraphic spiral glyph) fades up in the center, core brightening to peach-white, with a short Aurebesh string appearing to its right - the ignition signature. The camera then whips right (216522-216540 blurred) to the second gauge, now fully alive: yellow circuit-track outer ring with solder-pad dots, inner tick ring, dark amber turbine medallion in the center, a GREEN arc at upper-left and a BLUE arc wrapping the lower-left quadrant, three gold glyphs at 2 o'clock and a yellow alert box with stacked glyphs at 4 o'clock. Across 216558-216612 the arcs visibly grow clockwise (yellow tip extends past the green, blue lengthens) - power building over ~2 seconds. Cuts to a live-action hand plugging a cable in at ~216620.
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Status-by-color boot ramp: dormant = desaturated brick red outlines only; alive = saturated gold (#E8A020) ring, green (#3CB54A) and cobalt-blue (#3E6FD8) progress arcs that accrete clockwise; broken 'circuit-trace' ring with rounded tabs and pad dots; central sigil ignition acts as a splash/boot logo; lens-flare hotspot on the convex glass

uiSequences.label: Left gauge powers down (failure) while amber engine schematic flickers with fire
uiSequences.description: Two displays side by side. LEFT: the circular gauge now renders entirely in crimson - red broken ring, red tick marks, red alert wedge box with glyph pair at 4 o'clock, small glowing red dot at 6 o'clock, and the central orange sigil glowing softly with three tiny glyphs beside it. Over 216900-216972 it dies in stages: sigil vanishes (216918), ring fades to thin red outlines (216936), then the dome goes completely dark (216954-216972) - a system-failure power-down beat of about 3 seconds. RIGHT: the edge of the large oval screen shows a gold wireframe engine schematic whose interior flickers with orange flame-like light (fire onset), with light-yellow filled segment blocks along the bezel arc.
uiSequences.visualLanguage: All-red palette = degraded/failing channel (same ring geometry as the healthy gold gauge, recolored crimson); staged fade-out animation (content, then chrome, then black); neighbor screen keeps full gold wireframe with animated fire flicker inside the engine outline - color alone carries system state

uiSequences.label: Physical switch-panel insert: backlit square buttons and red indicator lamps
uiSequences.description: Live-action insert of the cockpit's mechanical panel as Anakin's hand reaches in: a column of square backlit push-buttons (green at top, amber, then red), chrome toggle switches and rotary knobs in a gunmetal plate, and to the right a loose constellation of small round indicator lamps glowing hot red, orange and yellow against near-black. Lit buttons read as jewel-like translucent plastic over incandescent bulbs.
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Practical hardware UI: saturated jewel-tone backlit squares (green/amber/red) with dark metal bezels, glowing red dome lamps with strong falloff, brushed/greebled military-surplus panel, very low ambient light so each lamp blooms - good reference for a 'physical toggle' skeuomorph row under a digital dashboard

uiSequences.label: ANCHOR: dual-engine schematic screen - fire flicker, blue energy bar fills, red alarm outline flashes
uiSequences.description: The clip's hero display, a large rounded-rectangle CRT recessed in finned grey metal. Layout: two vertical engine pods in thin gold wireframe flank a central cockpit-hub icon with bracket wings; faint amber polar-grid web in the background; three amber status dots top-center; down-pointing chevrons below the hub; yellow segment blocks arc along the left/right bezel. Evolution: at 217017-217026 the LEFT engine's interior flickers with animated orange-white flame (fire), no blue present. At 217044 a bright cyan-blue horizontally-striped band starts filling the RIGHT engine from the bottom (energy/coolant rerouting). By 217080 a two-line Aurebesh caption block appears top-center plus two small caption clusters lower-left/center, the hub shows yellow and grey-blue pill indicators, and the blue bar has grown to about two-thirds height. At 217098-217116 the entire LEFT engine silhouette is stroked in bright pulsing RED (the fire alarm), a small orange caption box lights below it, and the blue striped bar reaches full height - alarm and remedy peaking together before cutting to switch-flipping at ~217130.
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Thin 1-3 px gold/amber (#E8A020) wireframe schematics on deep brown-black; alert state = whole-silhouette red (#FF2A18) outline stroke that pulses, not a separate icon; progress = cyan-blue (#5FA8FF) bar with fine horizontal scanline stripes filling bottom-up inside the engine outline; Aurebesh caption typography in gold appears only when something needs explaining; bezel-mounted yellow segment arcs and three-dot LED row; CRT glow, halation, convex-glass bloom

uiSequences.label: Frantic switch-flipping inserts: lamps, toggles, striped lever
uiSequences.description: Series of dark live-action inserts after the alarm: a hand grips a red/white candy-striped circular lever/dial (217152), then sweeping handheld shots across panel rows (217188-217220) with lit red and yellow round lamps, white-tipped toggle switches, square amber/orange and red backlit buttons at top-left, and a chrome dome knob. Heavy motion blur in 217188 implies fast, urgent hand movement across the panel.
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Same practical hardware family as 216985-217012: near-black panel, hot red/amber/yellow indicator domes with bloom, jewel push-buttons, chrome toggles; striped red/white safety lever signals 'emergency control'; handheld blur conveys urgency - useful motion language for alarm-state dashboard transitions

firstHalf.nonUiSummary: Remaining frames are exterior podrace footage: desert-canyon racing, the pod's twin engines with purple energy-binder lightning, engine hardware close-ups, and Anakin helmet/goggles reaction shots.

secondHalf.nonUiSummary: Everything between the console shots is the repair/launch montage: Anakin in helmet and flip-down goggles in the cockpit, hands working levers, engine-nacelle spike close-ups (idle, then igniting with a flame burst around 218157), desert canyon arches, Sebulba's pod, and POV race footage with purple energy streaks.

uiSequences.label: Pre-flight toggle panel (physical indicator console)
uiSequences.description: Close-up of an oily gunmetal switch deck while a finger flips chrome teardrop toggles. Two bright red dome lamps glow at frame right, plus scattered amber/yellow dome lamps; an illuminated square rocker at upper-left glows hot orange-red; one small square red lamp sits mid-panel. 217257 moves closer: a knurled chrome rotary knob, ribbed copper coil below the switch row, yellow domes and one red dome lit. uiSequences.label: Main engine-status monitor: red fault clears, blue energy bars fill (anchor-style screen)
uiSequences.description: Rounded-square CRT monitor recessed in a weathered grey cast-metal bezel with ribbed vents, wiring harness pinned to the right. Screen shows twin podracer engine schematics as vertical wireframe columns. At 217473 the LEFT column is outlined in alarm RED while the right column is amber with a blue scanline bar; a warm orange glow with small glyph caption sits bottom-left; yellow arc segments mark screen center. By 217509 the red fault has cleared - both columns amber - and the center shows a yellow C-bracket arrow feeding a horizontal stream of 5-6 glowing orange capsule dots (power-transfer animation); the right column's blue bar drains/relocates. 217545-217577: BOTH columns now hold blue hatch-striped bars in their lower thirds while the orange capsule dots pulse and fade one by one (about one dot per 8-10 frames). Huttese rune header plus sub-caption sit top-center; three oval indicator dots (amber/yellow) across the top. A second circular gauge peeks in at frame right: concentric segmented amber rings with green/blue/yellow wedge segments and a single yellow dot. Ends ~217578 cutting back to Anakin.
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Black-brown screen ground with faint radial spider-web gridlines; thin single-weight amber/gold wireframe (#E8A020) with soft CRT bloom; alarm state = saturated red outline (#FF3322) on the affected engine only; energy bars = cyan-blue (#6EC1F0) with fine horizontal scanline hatching; power flow = orange glowing capsules (#FF8C2A) in a dotted row behind a yellow C-bracket arrow; typography = runic Huttese glyphs in amber, header-plus-caption scale; rounded-squircle bezel, ribbed heat-sink vents, visible cabling - lived-in CRT aesthetic.

uiSequences.label: Ignition button stack panel, first visit (cyan/amber/orange squares)
uiSequences.description: Tight shot of a vertical stack of three backlit translucent square push-buttons in rounded-square gunmetal wells: top = cyan/teal, middle = amber-yellow, bottom = red-orange. Right of the stack: a column of toggle switches (one with a brass wire-lock lever) and round dome lamps, 2-3 glowing bright red, others unlit olive. Far left: blue-grey metal knob and dial hardware. Anakin's hand wraps a black thumb-trigger lever between camera and panel and pushes it forward - reads as throttle/ignition arming. Button states stay constant; the story is told by hand motion plus the steady red domes. Ends between 217734 and 217743 (cut to engine spike).
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Backlit square jewel buttons with soft hotspot glow: cyan #2FB8C8, amber #FFA62E, orange-red #FF5A22; domes in pure red; dark desaturated bronze panel metal with scratches; deep shadow, warm key light from upper left; chunky industrial toggles, brass and steel fittings.

uiSequences.label: Ignition button stack panel, second visit (re-arm after stall - cyan button dimmed)
uiSequences.description: Same three-button stack from a wider, canted angle. New context on the left: chrome cylinders topped with a blue plastic wing-knob and a red T-handle. The top cyan button is now visibly DIMMER/darker (de-energized) than in the first visit, while the amber and red-orange buttons remain lit; additional red and orange dome lamps glow at lower-right. Anakin's hand repeatedly pumps/squeezes the central black lever - an engine re-start gesture during the stall. Lamp state difference between the two visits (bright cyan to dim cyan) is the key diegetic 'system down' cue. Ends between 218004 and 218013 (cut to engine spike).
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Identical hardware language to the first visit but cooler/dustier grade; dimmed cyan jewel = powered-down channel, persisting amber/orange jewels = standby; blue wing-knob and red T-handle add primary-color mechanical accents against bronze metal.

uiSequences.label: Main monitor engine boot-up: amber wireframe to green online state with sequential gold arc fill
uiSequences.description: The clip's hero UI animation. 218166-218175: the twin-engine schematic is monochrome gold/amber on near-black, columns empty except small blue scanline bars at the very bottom; center shows two grey-white curved coupling shapes flanking a bright yellow vertical bar; three oval indicators top-right (two dim amber, one bright yellow-green); at the left bezel edge a neighboring circular display sits dormant showing only thin RED wireframe arcs and glyphs on black. 218193: dimmest state - pure gold outlines, yellow corner brackets at mid-edges, downward chevron stack bottom-center, no fill anywhere. 218202: both engine columns REPAINT to neon mint-green wireframe with a soft green fill (engines back online) - the repaint completes in under ~9 frames (~0.4s at 24fps). 218211-218256: segmented arc tiles ringing the screen edge light up one by one to bright solid gold, symmetrically left/right (roughly one new segment per 10-15 frames, ~0.5s cadence), while the green columns brighten and the chevrons stay amber. By 218256 nearly the full peripheral arc ring is lit. Ends between 218256 and 218265 (cut to Anakin reacting).
uiSequences.visualLanguage: Boot-state grammar: OFF = thin gold outline (#C8881A) on black-brown; ONLINE = mint-green wireframe with glowing whitish-green core (#7CFA9C over #DFFFE8); progress = peripheral segmented arc tiles filling solid yellow-gold (#FFD23F) in sequence like a circular loading bar; persistent furniture = radial web gridlines, downward chevron stack, three oval status dots stepping dim-amber to bright yellow, yellow corner brackets; adjacent dormant gauge in skeletal red (#7A1010) supplies a 'cold system' contrast; all lines single-weight with CRT bloom and slight barrel distortion in the squircle bezel.

animation.name: Motion (motion.dev, formerly Framer Motion) — RECOMMENDED BACKBONE
animation.what: v12.40.0 (npm, published 2026-05-21), MIT, ~30M downloads/month. Hybrid engine: runs animations on WAAPI/ScrollTimeline natively for off-main-thread performance, falls back to JS for springs, interruptible keyframes, gestures. Springs are the default for transforms (type:'spring'), tweens for opacity. React API: <motion.div>, variants with staggerChildren, AnimatePresence for exit animations, layout prop for FLIP-style layout animations (panels reflowing smoothly when a worktree appears/disappears). Imperative animate() supports timeline sequencing (array segments with 'at' absolute/relative/label offsets), stagger(), and SVG line drawing via pathLength/pathOffset/pathSpacing on motion.path. Tree-shakeable: mini build 2.3kb, hybrid 18kb. Recent additions: ViewTimeline support, useFollowValue (spring-following motion values — ideal for gauge needles tracking telemetry).
animation.fitForPodracerDashboard: Best fit if the dashboard is React (it should be, given xyflow + component-heavy panels). layout/AnimatePresence solve the hard problems — alarm banners mounting/unmounting, panels rearranging as agent sessions spawn/die — that timeline libraries don't. useSpring/useFollowValue gives energy-fill bars and gauges physical overshoot for free. pathLength covers basic SVG wireframe draw-on.
animation.risks: Timeline ergonomics for long cinematic boot choreography are weaker than GSAP/anime.js (sequences exist but labels/nesting are less rich). Some premium components (Cursor, Ticker, AnimateNumber) are paid Motion+ — core library is fully MIT.

animation.name: anime.js v4 — RECOMMENDED CHOREOGRAPHY/SVG SPECIALIST (pair with Motion, or use solo if not React)
animation.what: v4.4.1 (npm, published 2026-04-30), MIT. v4 (April 2025) is a complete ESM-first modular rewrite: animate(), createTimeline() with labels and .call(), createTimer(), createSpring(), createScope() (scoped lifecycle for React/cleanup), createDraggable, onScroll. SVG module: svg.createDrawable() (stroke draw-on, replaces v3 setDashoffset), svg.createMotionPath(), svg.morphTo() (path morphing). v4.3 added createLayout() for layout-state animation; v4.4 added scrambleText() (character-scramble decode effect) and auto-grid stagger for 2D layouts. Framework-agnostic, tree-shakeable, plus a lighter WAAPI-backed module.
animation.fitForPodracerDashboard: The strongest tool for the cinematic layer: a single createTimeline() with labels ('power-on', 'systems-check', 'online') orchestrating staggered panel reveals, svg.createDrawable() drawing the amber podracer schematic line-by-line, and scrambleText() doing the decoding-readout boot text. This is almost a checklist of the podracer aesthetic. Works fine alongside React via createScope().
animation.risks: Imperative — needs ref/useEffect discipline inside React; smaller plugin ecosystem than GSAP; one-maintainer project (Julian Garnier), though release cadence through April 2026 is healthy.

animation.name: GSAP — strong alternative, now free, but third choice here
animation.what: v3.15.0 on npm. Since v3.13 (April 30, 2025, after the Webflow acquisition) GSAP is 100% free for commercial use including ALL formerly-paid Club plugins: DrawSVGPlugin (purpose-built wireframe draw-on), MorphSVG, SplitText, ScrollTrigger. Best-in-class nested timelines and easing. React integration via official useGSAP hook.
animation.fitForPodracerDashboard: DrawSVG + timelines would nail the boot sequence and schematics just as well as anime.js. Choose it if the team already knows GSAP.
animation.risks: Free but NOT OSI open source — custom 'Standard License' owned by Webflow (no fork rights; terms could theoretically change). Heavier than anime.js v4; less idiomatic in React than Motion. For a local-first quirky tool, MIT (Motion/anime) is cleaner.

animation.name: Verdict
animation.what: Use Motion v12 as the React-native foundation (layout animations, AnimatePresence alarms, spring-driven gauges/bars, WAAPI offload) + anime.js v4 for the boot-sequence timeline, SVG schematic draw-on, and scrambleText readouts. Both MIT, both tree-shakeable, combined cost well under GSAP+plugins. Skip raw WAAPI-only: no springs, no orchestration.
animation.fitForPodracerDashboard: Motion handles 'dashboard as living UI'; anime.js handles 'dashboard as movie prop'. The split maps exactly onto the product's two personalities.

charts.name: uPlot 1.6.32 (MIT) — RECOMMENDED for streaming telemetry lines
charts.what: Canvas-based micro-library (~50KB) by leeoniya (Grafana engineer). Benchmarks: streams 3,600 points at 60fps using ~10% CPU / 12MB RAM vs Chart.js (40%/77MB) and ECharts (70%/85MB); 166k points cold-start in 25ms. Update via setData() each rAF tick. Last npm publish 2025-03; stable/maintained, slow cadence. https://github.com/leeoniya/uPlot
charts.fit: The clear choice for buttery 60fps streaming line charts of agent/provider telemetry. Deliberately unstyled — you draw series, fills, and axes yourself, which is exactly what an amber-on-black CRT theme needs (custom stroke/fill hooks let you add glow gradients and 'energy fill' areas under lines). Canvas beats SVG decisively for streaming: no DOM churn, one repaint per frame.

charts.name: Apache ECharts 6.1.0 (Apache-2.0)
charts.what: Full-featured canvas+SVG charting; ECharts 6 (2025) added a refreshed default theme and built-in dark mode; rich gauge, radar, and heatmap types with smooth animation. https://echarts.apache.org
charts.fit: Use selectively for cockpit gauges/radar widgets where its built-in gauge type and animation save weeks — but not for high-rate streaming (7x uPlot's CPU). Theming to amber/CRT is straightforward via theme JSON.

charts.name: lightweight-charts 5.2.0 (TradingView, Apache-2.0)
charts.what: Canvas financial charts (candles, price scales), very fast, finance-domain API. https://www.tradingview.com/lightweight-charts/
charts.fit: Skip — its trading-desk idiom (price axes, time scales) fights the podracer aesthetic and uPlot already covers fast lines.

charts.name: visx 3.12.0 (Airbnb, MIT) and Observable Plot 0.6.17 (ISC)
charts.what: visx: low-level React+D3 SVG primitives; Plot: declarative exploratory plotting that re-renders the whole figure. https://airbnb.io/visx / https://observablehq.com/plot/
charts.fit: Neither suits 60fps streaming (SVG re-render model). visx is viable for static bespoke SVG charts that need filters/glow applied (SVG filters work on SVG charts, not canvas), e.g. a one-shot session-summary chart.

charts.name: @xyflow/react (React Flow) 12.11.0 (MIT) — RECOMMENDED for topology
charts.what: Node-based graph UI library, actively maintained (npm March 2026, docs April 2026). Built-in dark mode via colorMode prop, all default styles are CSS variables, fully custom React nodes/edges, animated edges, minimap, auto-layout via elkjs/dagre. https://reactflow.dev
charts.fit: Exactly right for the worktree/provider/pipeline topology map: each node is a custom React component, so nodes can be amber SVG wireframe panels with draw-on borders and live status LEDs; animated dashed edges read as 'energy conduits'. CSS-variable theming drops straight into a CRT token system.

fuiPatterns.pattern: Animated wireframe schematic draw-on (amber podracer blueprint)
fuiPatterns.howToBuild: Author the schematic as SVG with stroke-only paths. Normalize with pathLength="1" attribute, then animate stroke-dasharray/stroke-dashoffset from 1 to 0. Use anime.js svg.createDrawable() (handles measurement for you, supports partial start/end for 'scanning' effects), Motion's pathLength on motion.path, or GSAP DrawSVGPlugin. Stagger path groups (chassis, engines, energy binders) on a timeline so the schematic assembles subsystem-by-subsystem during boot.

For SVG strokes: filter with feGaussianBlur on SourceGraphic + feMerge stacking 1-2 blurred copies under the sharp original (classic neon-glow filter). For text/DOM: stacked text-shadow / drop-shadow() layers (tight bright + wide dim, e.g. 0 0 2px + 0 0 8px + 0 0 20px in the amber hue). PERFORMANCE RULE: never animate blur stdDeviation or filter radius per-frame — large-area Gaussian blur kills frame rate. Instead pre-render the glow layer and animate its opacity, or register a CSS @property custom property and pulse a glow-strength variable that only drives opacity/color.
fuiPatterns.reference: feGaussianBlur/feMerge: MDN SVG filter docs; CSS @property is Baseline across browsers

fuiPatterns.howToBuild: Pure CSS overlay, zero JS cost: a fixed pointer-events:none layer with repeating-linear-gradient(transparent 0 2px, rgba(0,0,0,.25) 2px 4px) for scanlines, a radial-gradient vignette, optional mix-blend-mode:overlay; subtle flicker via a slow opacity keyframe animation (compositor-only). Chromatic-aberration accents via offset red/cyan text-shadows on headings only. This works over live DOM — the key constraint is that WebGL postprocessing CANNOT sample live DOM content.

fuiPatterns.pattern: Full CRT shader (curvature, bloom, phosphor mask) — canvas regions only
fuiPatterns.howToBuild: Real barrel distortion/bloom needs WebGL fragment shaders, which can only post-process content already in a canvas. Use crt-fx or CRTFilter.js on canvas-rendered regions (e.g. wrap the uPlot chart canvas or a PixiJS background layer), or run the whole 'screen' inside one canvas if you go full-shader. Recommended architecture: DOM panels + CSS scanline overlay globally, shader CRT only on the canvas chart/background layers — best fidelity-to-effort ratio and keeps text crisp/accessible.
fuiPatterns.reference: https://github.com/stefanlegg/crt-fx (scanlines, phosphor masks, chromatic aberration, bloom), https://github.com/Ichiaka/CRTFilter

fuiPatterns.howToBuild: One master anime.js createTimeline() with labels: (1) black screen + power-on flash; (2) scanline overlay fades in; (3) schematic draw-on (createDrawable, staggered per subsystem); (4) panel frames stagger-reveal (clip-path or scaleY from a center line, stagger() with auto-grid); (5) boot text via scrambleText()/typewriter with WebAudio chirps per line; (6) live data fades in and SSE subscription starts. Gate the timeline on document.fonts.ready + first status snapshot so it never reveals empty panels. Play once per session (sessionStorage flag), provide a skip on click, and swap to an instant variant under prefers-reduced-motion. Arwes's Animator system (cascading parent→child enter/exit flows) is the best architectural reference for making every panel know its place in the cascade.

Model alarm as a cockpit-wide state token (nominal-amber → caution → alarm-red) flowing through CSS variables so every panel reacts (border hues, glow color, gauge accents) rather than spawning corporate toasts. Alarm visual: pulsing border/glow via animated @property variable + an AnimatePresence-mounted klaxon banner; audio chirp via WebAudio. HARD CONSTRAINT: keep any flashing at or under 3 flashes/second and avoid full-screen red strobes (WCAG 2.3.1 photosensitive seizure threshold) — a 1Hz breathe/pulse reads more cinematic anyway. Persist the alarm in a 'master caution' indicator that stays lit until acknowledged, like real cockpits.
fuiPatterns.reference: WCAG 2.3.1 Three Flashes or Below Threshold

fuiPatterns.howToBuild: Layered bar: dark track + gradient fill (deep blue → electric cyan) + a narrow leading-edge glow element. Drive width/scaleX with Motion useSpring/useFollowValue so value changes overshoot slightly like a physical gauge; add a slow animated background-position shimmer on the fill (compositor-friendly) for the 'energy flowing' look. For segmented podracer-style bars, render N cells and stagger their ignition with anime.js.

fuiPatterns.pattern: Arwes as a source to mine, not a dependency
fuiPatterns.howToBuild: Arwes (https://github.com/arwes/arwes, 7.5k stars) is the canonical sci-fi UI framework: frames (SVG corner-bracket/octagon panel borders), animator cascades, text transition effects, and bleeps (sound manager). BUT: still 1.0.0-alpha; latest npm next build @arwes/react 1.0.0-next.25020502 published Feb 2025 (16 months stale); explicitly 'not production ready'; incompatible with React strict mode and RSC. Verdict: do not build on it — copy its frame SVG geometry ideas and its animator/bleeps architecture into your own ~200-line equivalents. Its vanilla sub-packages (@arwes/frames, @arwes/bleeps) are the least risky pieces if you must import something.

From their film FUI practice: (1) motion-first — design the animation behavior before the static comp, it changes the layout; (2) every graphic serves the narrative — each panel should answer a real operator question (what phase? what's burning?) before being decorative; (3) coherence — one type family, one grid, one glow language across all panels so the cockpit feels like one machine.

tech.hyperframes: HyperFrames (https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes, https://hyperframes.app) is HeyGen's open-source (Apache-2.0, TypeScript, Node 22+) 'agent-native' HTML-to-VIDEO renderer — current v0.6.88 as of June 9, 2026, very active (1,650+ commits). You write an HTML document whose animations are driven by CSS/GSAP/Lottie/Three.js plus timing data-attributes; it seeks each frame deterministically in headless Chrome (virtual clock, zero dropped frames) and encodes MP4/MOV/WebM with FFmpeg, mixing audio. It is strictly an OFFLINE rendering pipeline for producing video files (explainers, demos, data-viz clips) — it is NOT a UI framework, has no runtime/live-data capability, and does NOT fit as a building block for a live dashboard. Adjacent fit only: because your dashboard is already HTML/CSS animation, you could reuse the same components to render cinematic MP4 'mission replay' videos of completed agent sessions for sharing — a genuinely on-brand bonus feature, not part of the dashboard itself.
tech.transport: RECOMMENDATION: SSE (Server-Sent Events), one multiplexed stream — not WebSocket, not polling. Rationale for this exact product (local FastAPI/uvicorn tailing JSONL + status JSON): (1) traffic is purely server→client; the only client→server actions (acknowledge alarm, open worktree) are fine as plain POSTs, so WebSocket's bidirectionality buys nothing while costing manual reconnection logic, heartbeat handling, and message framing. (2) Browser EventSource reconnects AUTOMATICALLY and sends the Last-Event-ID header on reconnect — the built-in backfill hook. (3) FastAPI now ships first-class SSE: as of FastAPI 0.135.0, fastapi.sse provides EventSourceResponse (yield items from an async generator, auto JSON-encoded) and ServerSentEvent (data/event/id/retry fields), with automatic 15s keep-alive ping comments and Cache-Control: no-cache (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/server-sent-events/). On older FastAPI, sse-starlette (https://github.com/sysid/sse-starlette) is the same pattern. CONCRETE DESIGN: (a) Snapshot + delta: on page load (and after every reconnect) GET /api/status for the full status JSON, then subscribe to /api/events for deltas — or have the server emit a full snapshot as the first SSE event per connection; this makes reconnects self-healing. (b) Event IDs from the JSONL itself: use byte offset or line number per log file (e.g. id = 'sessions.jsonl:48213'); the Last-Event-ID header (read via Header() param) tells you exactly where to resume tailing — seek, replay missed lines, continue. (c) Tail JSONL with an async loop holding a file-position cursor (or watchfiles for FS notification) yielding ServerSentEvent(event='lifecycle'|'provider'|'memory'|'alarm', data=..., id=...). (d) ONE EventSource, named event types, fan out client-side (addEventListener per type) — uvicorn speaks HTTP/1.1 and browsers cap ~6 connections per origin, so per-panel EventSources will starve the tab. (e) Set retry: 2000 so reconnect feels instant locally; render a diegetic 'SIGNAL LOST' flicker state while EventSource.readyState is CONNECTING — the failure mode becomes part of the cockpit fiction. (f) Skip polling entirely; only reach for WebSocket later if you add high-frequency client→server control (you won't). Note: EventSource can't send custom headers/POST bodies — irrelevant on localhost; @microsoft/fetch-event-source exists if that ever changes.
wildcards: WebAudio synthesized cockpit audio with zero assets: OscillatorNode (square/saw for klaxons, sine for confirmations) + GainNode exponential decay envelopes gives you boot chirps, keystroke ticks, and a two-tone alarm in ~40 lines; frequency-ramp an oscillator for the 'power-up sweep'. Gotcha: AudioContext only starts after a user gesture (autoplay policy) — make the boot sequence start from a big diegetic 'IGNITION' button click, which legitimizes audio for the whole session. Arwes's @arwes/bleeps package is a ready-made sci-fi sound manager if you'd rather not hand-roll. (MDN Web Audio advanced techniques: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Audio_API/Advanced_techniques)

anime.js v4.4 scrambleText() as a signature effect: every value change on critical readouts (phase names, branch names) decodes through a brief character-scramble — instantly reads as 'alien cockpit telemetry' and costs one function call.

PixiJS v8.19 (MIT, WebGPU+WebGL, experimental Canvas fallback; WebGL is the stable default since 8.1) as a single full-viewport background layer running a cheap fragment shader — engine heat-haze, drifting Tatooine dust, or phosphor noise — behind the DOM panels. Keep all content in DOM; the shader is pure atmosphere, pausable under prefers-reduced-motion. (https://pixijs.com/blog/8.16.0)

View Transitions API (same-document) is now cross-browser — Chrome 111+, Safari 18+, Firefox 144+ — so full cockpit 'mode switches' (overview ↔ session detail) can be a document.startViewTransition with a custom CRT wipe (::view-transition-old/new animated with a scanline mask) in ~20 lines, no router library. (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/View_Transition_API, https://caniuse.com/view-transitions)

CSS @property registered custom properties: register --glow-strength and --scan-pos as real animatable types and the browser interpolates gradients/glows natively on the compositor — pulsing alarm glows and roaming scanner lines without JS per-frame work.
OffscreenCanvas + Web Worker for the uPlot telemetry charts if the main thread ever gets busy with React renders during event bursts — guarantees the 60fps line keeps scrolling even mid-rerender.

HyperFrames 'mission replay' export: since the dashboard is already HTML/CSS animation, pipe a completed session's event log through the same components into HeyGen's HyperFrames to render a deterministic MP4 of the run — shareable cinematic replays of an agent's session, very podracer. (https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes)

prefers-reduced-motion as a feature, not a chore: ship a 'CALM COCKPIT' toggle (instant boot, static glows, no flicker, audio off) — doubles as the accessibility story and the long-day ergonomics story.
